title: Whisky Clubs and Tasting Societies | Craft Beer School
desc: How whisky clubs and tasting societies work: sharing bottles, formats that teach, running a good tasting and the legal side of meeting in India.
teaser: Ten people sharing one bottle each get 75 ml of something they would never buy alone. That is the case for a whisky club.
standfirst: A whisky club is the cheapest way to taste widely and the fastest way to train a palate. It works best with a little structure. Here is how clubs run, what formats work and what to watch in India.
sections: A club is the cheapest way to taste widely

The arithmetic is simple. A 750 ml bottle shared between ten members gives each person 75 ml, enough for two proper tasting pours. If each member brings or funds one bottle a month, everyone tastes ten whiskies for the price of one.

That matters in India, where good whisky is expensive and state taxes make imported bottles dearer still. A club lets you taste a peated Islay malt, a bourbon and an Indian single malt in one evening without owning any of them.

A club that just opens whatever turns up becomes a party. One with a theme becomes a school. Formats that work well include:

  • Regional nights. Speyside against Islay, or Scotch against Indian single malt.
  • Cask nights. The same spirit from bourbon, sherry and wine casks.
  • Blind flights. Bottles in paper bags, guesses before the reveal.
  • Members' choice. Each person presents one whisky and explains why.

Four to six whiskies is plenty for one evening. More than that and the later glasses blur into each other. A theme also makes buying easier, because each member knows what to look for. Write the theme and the bottle list in the group chat a week ahead so nobody turns up with a duplicate.

Use tulip-shaped nosing glasses, one per whisky if you can. Pour 15 to 20 ml. Put a jug of water and a few pipettes on the table so people can add drops after the first taste. Order the flight from light to heavy, with peated and cask strength whiskies last.

A simple scoring sheet helps: nose, palate, finish and an overall mark. The scores matter less than the discussion they start. Our guides to hosting a tasting at home and writing tasting notes cover the set-up in detail.

Labels shape what we taste. Tell people a whisky is 18 years old and expensive and many will find more in it. Pour it blind and the conversation changes.

One member pours each whisky into numbered glasses out of sight. Everyone writes notes and a guess before the reveal. It is humbling and it is the fastest way to learn what you actually like rather than what you think you should like.

Liquor rules in India are set by each state and they change. A private tasting at someone's home is different from an event at a hired venue. Serving alcohol at an event may need a temporary or occasional licence from the state excise department. Hotels and licensed bars can host under their own licences.

Collecting money from members to buy whisky can look like selling liquor, which needs a licence. Many clubs keep things simple by having each member buy and bring a bottle. Check the current rules in your state before you formalise anything. This is not legal advice.

The best clubs welcome beginners. Nobody should feel stupid for saying a whisky smells of mango or that they cannot find the smoke. Snobbery kills a club faster than bad whisky.

Mixed groups work well. A club with a few experienced tasters and a few curious beginners learns faster than one where everyone already agrees. Beginners ask the questions that experienced drinkers have stopped asking.

Keep pours small and the count sensible. Put spit cups on the table, serve food and offer good non-alcoholic drinks. Agree before every meeting how people are getting home. Nobody drives after a tasting.

Clubs fade when one person does all the work. Rotate the host and the theme each month. Keep a shared record of what was tasted, the scores and who brought what. After a year you will have a useful map of the group's tastes.

Some clubs invite a guest speaker, perhaps a brand ambassador or a distiller, once or twice a year. That brings new knowledge and new bottles to the table.
Start with four friends and three bottles

You do not need a society to begin. Invite three friends who are curious about whisky. Ask each to bring one bottle that fits a simple theme, such as three different cask types. Pour 15 ml of each, taste them in order, write notes and compare.

If the evening works, set a date and a theme for the next one before anyone goes home. That is how most clubs start.
faqs: How does a whisky club share costs?
Members share bottles. A 750 ml bottle split between ten people gives each 75 ml, so everyone tastes widely for the price of one bottle.
Do I need a licence to run a whisky club in India?
It depends on your state and the format. Events at venues may need an occasional licence and collecting money for alcohol can count as selling. Check with the state excise department.
How many whiskies should a club tasting include?
Four to six whiskies at 15 to 20 ml each is plenty for one evening.
